title: Journal of Experimental Psychology: General - Vol 155, Iss 9

items.title: Attentional engagement enhances encoding-based discrimination in aging.
items.content: The present study investigated how goal-directed attention modulates age-related declines in the ability to behaviorally differentiate overlapping stimuli in memory. Participants completed a perceptual discrimination task involving relevant (attention-prioritized) and irrelevant items, followed by a surprise memory test. Using a sensitive gaze-based measure, we found that directing attention to prioritized stimuli enabled older adults to discriminate among similar items at levels comparable to young adults. Gaze similarity also predicted memory performance, with age differences emerging only during explicit testing. These findings demonstrate that attentional engagement and assessment method critically shape age-related changes in discriminating overlapping stimuli. items.title: Object perception encodes mutually exclusive possibilities.
items.content: Human adults represent and reason about possibilities: multiple, mutually exclusive, nonactual ways the world could be. It is debated whether this is a late-developing, human-specific capacity and whether it requires natural language. We propose that instead of a unitary high-level capacity, multiple cognitive capacities might independently represent possibilities in different ways and with different properties. Our case study is object perception, a capacity shared with infants and nonhuman animals. Using methods that tap specifically into visual processes, across four experiments (N = 160), we found possibility representations in vision tasks that do not involve high-level reasoning or language. In Experiments 1 and 2, we found evidence for the visual encoding of possible object identities: When there were two possible ways that features might map onto visual objects, both possible mappings were primed. In Experiment 3, we found that visual feature binding is a necessary precondition for such priming, ruling out low-level associative and high-level reasoning-based alternatives. Finally, in Experiment 4, we discovered that the visual system cannot encode one visual object possibly being at two possible locations. This pattern helps to explain a host of previous findings from the comparative and developmental literature and suggests that the unit of analysis for possibility representations should be the cognitive capacity rather than the agent. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

items.title: Task similarity increases difficulty in maintaining but not in switching between tasks.
items.content: Switching tasks and adapting to new situations by appropriately allocating mental resources is crucial for interacting with the world around us. This ability requires cognitive control and includes several operations such as maintaining and modifying task goals, allocating attention to the relevant stimulus, and selecting the appropriate motor command. Surprisingly, although we know that switching between tasks incurs costs, whether the type of activity itself makes any difference has rarely been investigated. This study uses an innovative, well-controlled paradigm that keeps response rules and stimulus set constant across tasks to specifically test how efficiently humans switch between tasks sharing similar versus dissimilar neural processes. We assessed the efficiency of transient and global cognitive control by comparing participants’ switch costs, the efficiency of task reconfiguration, and mixing costs, the efficiency of task maintenance. In four experiments, employing different stimuli and tasks, the results consistently show that increased similarity between pairs of tasks increased the difficulty in maintaining the tasks but not in switching between them. This dissociation confirms that switch and mixing costs are independent processes. Importantly, the overlap in neural processing between tasks appears to be detrimental in simultaneously maintaining tasks, potentially due to competition or interference. Distinct task sets are more efficient to maintain than similar ones. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

items.title: Correction to “does affective processing require awareness? On the use of the perceptual awareness scale in response priming research” by wentura et al. (2025).
items.content: Reports an error in "Does affective processing require awareness? On the use of the Perceptual Awareness Scale in response priming research" by Dirk Wentura, Michaela Rohr and Markus Kiefer (Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2025[Jan], Vol 154[1], 128-151; see record ). follow up analysis of the data showed the original was incorrect. The data has been corrected. (The following abstract of the original article appeared in record .) Masked priming paradigms are frequently used to shine light on the processes of nonconscious cognition. Introducing a new method to this field, Lähteenmäki et al. (2015) claimed that affective priming requires awareness. Specifically, they administered a subjective rating task after the priming task in each trial to directly assess awareness of the prime. Their main result was a lack of priming for subjectively unaware primes. In four experiments, we compared their method with the traditional paradigm, that is, a single-task priming phase followed by a direct test of prime recognition. We used faces with anger versus sadness expressions as primes and targets; emotion categorization was the task. In contrast to Lähteenmäki et al., primes and targets were drawn from different sets, such that priming effects can be unequivocally attributed to the processing of evaluative features. In Experiments 1a, b, we followed their approach of using different prime durations to produce variance in awareness ratings. With a duration of 40 ms, significant priming effects for subjectively unaware primes were found. This duration was also associated with priming effects in the traditional paradigm with near-zero objective prime categorization, suggesting that priming does not require awareness. In Experiment 2a, employing a constant 40-ms duration, we replicated the traditional effect. However, the parallel Experiment 2b with subjective awareness ratings produced a null result at a sharply increased response time level. We conclude that the claim that affective processing requires awareness is not justified. Subjective trial-by-trial visibility ratings can severely alter processing strategies in response priming paradigms. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

items.title: A right and a privilege? Examining White americans’ construal of voting as a privilege, anti-Black attitudes, and voter suppression support.
items.content: Although Americans express commitment to democratic norms, nearly half of White Americans prefer to define voting as a privilege that can be limited among U.S. citizens. Across four studies (total  = 10,016), we examine how White Americans construe the concept of voting as an exclusionary privilege to illuminate when White Americans are likely to support restricting voter access. In Study 1, we find that White Americans’ perception of voting as a privilege is tied to seeing racism as less of an important social issue today and a greater focus on restricting voting, a pattern not observed among Black Americans. Study 2 shows that White Americans can construe voting as both a privilege and a right. Yet, only the perception of voting as a privilege (but not as a right) mediates the direct effect of anti-Black attitudes on support for policies that suppress voting legally (e.g., voter ID laws) and illegally (e.g., literacy tests). In Studies 3 and 4, we experimentally manipulate White Americans’ prescriptive beliefs about voting and find that shifting beliefs about whether voting should be a privilege or a right can, in turn, shift support for voter access policies. Taken together, White Americans’ construal of voting as a privilege is uniquely and consequentially tied to negative racial attitudes and support for policies that disproportionately suppress voting among marginalized racial outgroups. Implications for how construing core civic processes as a privilege may operate as a race-neutral cover for dominant groups to maintain group power are discussed. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

items.title: Developmental trajectories of vigilance in childhood and adolescence: Disentangling underlying mechanisms through behavioral modeling.
items.content: Sustained attention is crucial for daily functioning, yet research on vigilance development from childhood to early adulthood has yielded inconsistent findings. These discrepancies arise partly from the use of tasks with different vigilance demands and from limitations in the indices of sensitivity and response criterion used. This study examines vigilance development in a large sample of children, adolescents, and young adults (N = 809) using a novel, fine-grained analytical approach. Performance in executive vigilance was modeled using logistic curves (hits and false alarms), while arousal vigilance based on response speed was assessed using ex-Gaussian distributions (reaction times). Results showed that children’s responses became faster, less variable, and less prone to extreme reaction times throughout development, stabilizing by late adolescence. For executive vigilance, a newly identified two-phase developmental pattern emerged. While vigilance decrement in childhood and early adolescence appears to stem from limitations in the ability to control attentional resources, during later developmental stages, the decline may increasingly reflect a reallocation of resources toward mind wandering, resulting in more frequent attentional lapses. These findings underscore the value of advanced behavioral modeling for characterizing developmental trajectories of vigilance and provide new insights into its underlying mechanisms. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

items.title: Correction to “The spontaneous prioritization of ‘unfinishedness’ in perception: A visual Zeigarnik effect” by Ongchoco et al. (2026).
items.content: Reports an error in "The spontaneous prioritization of “unfinishedness” in perception: A visual Zeigarnik effect" by Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Kimberly W. Wong and Brian J. Scholl (Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2026[Mar], Vol 155[3], 649-655; see record ). In the article “The Spontaneous Prioritization of ‘Unfinishedness’ in Perception: A Visual Zeigarnik Effect” by Joan Danielle K. Ongchoco, Kimberly W. Wong, and Brian J. Scholl (Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 2026, Vol. 155, No. 3, pp. 649–655. https://doi.org/10.1037/xge0001884), there was a coding bug in the shuffling function. As a result,the individual mazes were not randomly ordered or counterbalanced across conditions, as was stated in the paper. (The following abstract of the original article appeared in record .) The events that occupy our thoughts in an especially persistent way are often those that are unfinished—from half-written papers to unfolded laundry. These events seem to also be privileged in memory, as in the “Zeigarnik effect”: When people carry out various tasks, but some are never finished due to extrinsic interruptions, memory tends to be better for those tasks that were unfinished. But just how foundational is this sort of “unfinishedness” in mental life? The Zeigarnik effect is often explained by appeal to the salience of goals or the weight of obligation, but might unfinishedness also be spontaneously prioritized even in visual processing—independent of these high-level social/motivational factors? Across four experiments ( = 120), observers viewed paths that gradually unfolded through mazes, from a start point to an end point. Probes briefly appeared along the path, and observers later simply reproduced their positions. Critically, each path either reached its end point or stopped shortly before—remaining visually unfinished. Although this manipulation was entirely task-irrelevant, it greatly influenced performance—with more precise reproductions on unfinished trials. This same pattern held across multiple experiments, even while carefully controlling for various lower level visual properties, and it generalized across different types of displays. This new shows how vision extracts an unexpectedly rich property that is usually associated with higher level thought, and how the unfinishedness of events is privileged in the mind at a deep level. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

items.title: Verbal recoding underlies visual ambiguity resolution, even in a nonlinguistic context.
items.content: In language, word order can be used to help disambiguate the grammatical category (noun, verb, etc.) to which an unfamiliar or ambiguous word belongs. We have recently demonstrated that the order of stimuli impacts how ambiguous stimuli are subsequently categorized, even in a nonlinguistic context. However, it remains possible that participants may linguistically recode these stimuli (i.e., giving abstract shapes “names”), such that this effect is still based in the language system. Here, we adapted our previous nonlinguistic paradigm assessing the impact of sequence order on categorization but with the addition of two interference conditions: one interfering with phonological systems of linguistic recoding and the other with visuospatial memory. We found that while the nonlinguistic, visuospatial interference task had no impact on the sequence categorization effect, the linguistic interference task substantially reduced this effect. These results suggest that even though the task uses nonlinguistic stimuli, participants appeared to recode this information linguistically and, thus, that this effect may be a feature of language, rather than a more domain-general cognitive process. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)

items.title: Complex and beautiful: Distinct black history knowledge types drive interpretative similarity of, and emotional responses to, modern and historical racism among black people.
items.content: Black history knowledge (BHK) is considered a powerful tool for Black people in the United States. Although scholars have proposed theoretical subdomains of BHK, little experimental work has investigated these different components, in tandem, to understand their benefits. Here, we investigate how two of these components—critical BHK (knowledge of historically documented anti-Black racism) and celebratory BHK (knowledge of historically documented Black achievement)—may facilitate Black people’s interpretative similarity of, and adaptive emotionality in response to, depictions of anti-Black racism in distinct temporal contexts. We examined the impact of preexisting critical and celebratory BHK on Black people’s (N = 118) written interpretations and emotional responses to two video clips showing salient depictions of anti-Black racism in modern versus historical contexts (between-subjects). Latent semantic analysis–based representational similarity analyses were used to map correlations between similar interpretations and similar BHK scores; follow-up Linguistic Inventory and Word Count analyses determined the effects of BHK on racism language in interpretations and emotion language in emotional responses. Similar critical (but not celebratory) BHK predicted interpretative similarity of modern anti-Black racism—with higher critical (but not celebratory) BHK related to the explicit naming of racism. Although similar, accurate knowledge of both BHK types predicted interpretative similarity of the historical clip, neither BHK type was related to racism language. While neither BHK type affected negative emotions elicited by either clip, those with higher celebratory BHK expressed fewer positive emotions after witnessing the modern clip, which may be considered adaptive. Our results suggest dissociable benefits of preexisting critical versus celebratory BHK for Black people. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved)
